facts.statement: A partial skeleton of Dracopelta was discovered in 1963 or early 1964 during road construction between Barril and Praia da Assenta.
facts.quote: In 1963 or, more likely, early 1964, a partial skeleton was discovered during road construction works between the village of Barril and Praia da Assenta.

facts.statement: Georges Zbyszewski and Octávio da Veiga Ferreir organized the excavation of the Dracopelta specimen in December 1964.
facts.quote: Georges Zbyszewski and Octávio da Veiga Ferreir organized the excavation and extraction of the specimen in December 1964.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen includes dorsal vertebrae, ribs, osteoderms, an incomplete foot, and unpublished bones such as a tibia and femur.
facts.quote: The holotype specimen, MG 3 (formerly IGM 5787 and IGM 3), consists of dorsal vertebrae, articulated proximal ribs, osteoderms, an incomplete autopodium and unpublished material including a tibia, femur, and an ossified tendon.

facts.statement: The genus name Dracopelta combines the Latin word for dragon and the Greek word for small shield.
facts.quote: The generic name, Dracopelta, is derived from the Latin word draco (dragon) and the Greek word πέλτη, pelte, (Latinised to pelta), "small shield".

facts.statement: The species name zbyszewskii honors Georges Zbyszewski for his research on Portuguese fossil vertebrates.
facts.quote: The specific name, zbyszewskii, honours Georges Zbyszewski, after his research on fossil vertebrates from Portugal.

facts.statement: A nearly complete ankylosaur specimen with a skull, vertebrae, ribs, and a pelvic shield was reported in 2019 from the Lourinhã Formation.
facts.quote: In 2019, a specimen of an ankylosaur consisting of a nearly complete skull, articulated dorsal vertebrae, proximal half of ribs, articulated anterior caudal vertebrae, mostly complete and articulated synsacrum, fragments of disarticulated and broken ribs, femora, partial ilia with attached pelvic shield, humerus, partial scapulocoracoid, tendons mostly attached to vertebrae, and osteoderms from the Lourinhã Formation was reported.

facts.statement: Gregory S. Paul estimated Dracopelta to be 3 meters long and weigh 300 kilograms in 2010.
facts.quote: In 2010, Gregory S. Paul estimated the body length of Dracopelta at 3 m and its weight at 300 kg.

facts.statement: A later publication suggested Dracopelta could have been between 4 and 6 meters long.
facts.quote: A later publication suggested a greater length of 4 - 6 m.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen represents an adult Dracopelta.
facts.quote: The holotype specimen represents an adult individual.

facts.statement: Dracopelta had gently curved dorsal ribs indicating a broad back similar to other ankylosaurs.
facts.quote: The dorsal ribs are gently curved which indicates that the back was broad, much like that of other ankylosaurs, Dryosaurus and Camptosaurus, and the base is at about the same level as the postzygapophyses and prezygapophyses.

facts.statement: The holotype preserves ossified tendons, a feature also found in ankylosaurs, ornithopods, and possibly Scelidosaurus.
facts.quote: The holotype preserves ossified tendons which is a feature seen in ankylosaurs, ornithopods and possibly Scelidosaurus.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest Dracopelta may have had cursorial adaptations based on its autopodial structure resembling that of Scutellosaurus and Scelidosaurus.
facts.quote: The authors interpreted that Dracopelta may have had cursorial adaptations as the autopodial structure falls into the metapodial range of the basal thyreophorans Scutellosaurus and Scelidosaurus, which were probably subcursorial.

facts.statement: Galton originally classified Dracopelta in Nodosauridae in 1980 based on osteoderm morphology.
facts.quote: Galton (1980) originally assigned Dracopelta to Nodosauridae, based on the morphology of the osteoderms.

facts.statement: Vickaryous et al. considered Dracopelta as Ankylosauria incertae sedis, while Carpenter classified it as a nomen dubium within Polacanthidae incertae sedis.
facts.quote: Vickaryous et al. (2004) interpreted Dracopelta as Ankylosauria incertae sedis while Carpenter (2001) considered it as a nomen dubium based on the lack off diagnostic characteristic of the holotype specimen and assigned it as Polacanthidae incertae sedis based on the similarities between Gargoyleosaurus and Gastonia in osteoderm morphology.

facts.statement: Suberbiola et al. considered Dracopelta a valid taxon based on unique phalangeal and osteoderm morphology.
facts.quote: Suberbiola et al. (2005) were unable to recognize any polacanthid or nodosaurid characteristics and considered Dracopelta as a valid taxon based on the presence of proximal phalanges II and III as long as wide and distinctive osteoderm morphology.

facts.statement: Dracopelta lived during the Late Jurassic (152.1-145.0 Ma) in the Lourinhã Formation of Portugal.
facts.quote: Dracopelta (meaning "dragon shield") is a monospecific genus of ankylosaurian dinosaur that lived during the Late Jurassic (uppermost lower Tithonian-upper Tithonian, 152.1-145.0 Ma) in what is now the Lourinhã Formation, Portugal.

facts.statement: The holotype was found in the Assenta Member of the Lourinhã Formation dating to the uppermost lower and upper Tithonian stages.
facts.quote: The holotype specimen of Dracopelta was obtained from a layer from the Assenta Member of the Lourinhã Formation, which dates to the uppermost lower and upper Tithonian stage of the Late Jurassic.

facts.statement: The Assenta Member represents a fluvial environment with preserved coalified plant fragments.
facts.quote: The member represents a fluvial channel and preserves small coalified plant fragments.

facts.statement: Dracopelta coexisted with Lusovenator, turiasaurian sauropods, crocodylomorphs, and another indeterminate ankylosaur.
facts.quote: Dracopelta would have coexisted with the carcharodontosaurian Lusovenator, indeterminate turiasaurian sauropods, indeterminate crocodylomorphs, and an indeterminate ankylosaur, which may represent a second and more complete specimen of Dracopelta.

facts.statement: Dracopelta is the first recognized ankylosaurid from the Late Jurassic and one of the oldest genera referred to Ankylosauria.
facts.quote: Dracopelta es el primer anquilosáurido reconocido del Jurásico tardío y los restos pertenecen a uno de los más antiguos géneros referidos a Ankylosauria.

facts.statement: Despite partial remains, Dracopelta is estimated to be around 2 meters long and was likely a quadrupedal herbivore.
facts.quote: A pesar de lo dificultoso de estimar el tamaño a partir de restos parciales, se cree que llegó a medir alrededor de 2 metros de largo, y seguramente fue un herbívoro cuadrúpedo.

facts.statement: Dracopelta may share close affinities with Gargoyleosaurus or Mymoorapelta due to faunal similarities.
facts.quote: Due to the close proximities between the fauna of the Morrison Formation and Lourinhã Formation, Dracopelta might share close affinities with Gargoyleosaurus or Mymoorapelta.

rejected.statement: It is debated whether the 2019 specimen represents a more complete Dracopelta or a new taxon.
rejected.quote: The specimen is currently being studied on to clarify if it represents an additional, more complete specimen, of Dracopelta or a new taxon.
